finding.claim: Stored (two-hop) blind SSRF. The attacker-supplied callbackUrl is saved by subscribe() with no validation. notifyAll() later sends a POST to every stored URL, so an attacker can make the server send requests to loopback, RFC-1918 or cloud-metadata addresses such as http://169.254.169.254/. The response is discarded, so it is blind SSRF, but an attacker can still probe ports and hosts and deliver the payload to internal services. Severity: HIGH under Check 4 if /subscribe is unauthenticated or low-privilege, otherwise MEDIUM because it is blind. No auth is visible in the code. The scheduler runs every minute with no re-validation at fetch time. The default Java HttpClient does not follow redirects, so redirect risk is not an additional factor.
finding.source: callbackUrl parameter of POST /subscribe (Jobs.subscribe, body field callbackUrl)

trace.note: POST /subscribe body: name, callbackUrl, which is user input
subscriptions.put(name, callbackUrl) stores the URL unvalidated
URI.create(cb) uses the stored URL with no scheme or host check
client.send() dispatches the POST with the payload, and the response is discarded

finding.guards_checked: No scheme or host allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local IP blocking, and no re-validation in subscribe() or notifyAll(). No authentication code in the file; I could not confirm whether the endpoint is authenticated. HttpClient.newHttpClient() uses the default redirect policy (NEVER), so redirects are not followed. No in-repo egress controls (CIDR) were found.

verdict.reason: src/Jobs.java:14 stores callbackUrl unvalidated and src/Jobs.java:21 passes it to URI.create and client.send at :24 with no scheme, host or IP check (the only regex guard, at :30, is in thumb() and not on this path); the file shows no authentication on /subscribe, and the response is discarded, so this is blind SSRF.
